answer:
R + W > N guarantees intersection, not freshness. Every read quorum of R replicas must share at least one replica with the W replicas that acknowledged the newest write, so that version is present among the responses — provided both operations use the same replica set and the write actually reached W replicas. Intersection is necessary: with R + W ≤ N the sets can be disjoint and no respondent can supply the value. It is not sufficient, because a replica holding the newest copy does not force the response that copy.

Sufficiency needs more. The write must really be durable on W replicas; a failed or partial write leaves only older versions to intersect. Membership must be strict: Dynamo and Riak sloppy quorums route to fallback nodes, so the R respondents and W acknowledgers can be different sets. The reader must select the newest version: Cassandra's last-write-wins timestamps assume a total order, Dynamo and Riak can return concurrent siblings, and clock skew can invert that order. Replica movement during membership change can also break old/new overlap. Read repair and hinted handoff are best-effort; anti-entropy converges only eventually. A leader simplifies ordering but still needs a majority; per-session read-your-writes is a separate obligation. Evidence is documentation and a 2007 paper, not an implementation test.

evidence.claim: R + W > N gives set intersection only; the reader must still select the highest version and repair stale replicas.
evidence.note: Observed: 'when R + W > N and membership is correctly configured, the sets intersect, but the reader must select the highest version and repair stale replicas'; 'A read with too small R can return stale data.' Hence necessity.

evidence.claim: Overlap is necessary but not sufficient for freshness; a read intersecting the write quorum can still return stale data when the write failed, membership was sloppy, or the selector ignores the newest replica.
evidence.note: Observed, near-verbatim: 'Overlap is necessary but not sufficient for freshness' and the three stale-return conditions listed in Failure and recovery.

evidence.claim: Sloppy quorum in Dynamo and Riak sends requests to fallback nodes instead of enforcing strict membership, so acknowledged and read sets need not be the same replica set.
evidence.note: Observed; book labels it summarized from cited sections, not quoted verbatim. Riak documents sloppy quorum as failover mode, strict quorum as an option.

evidence.claim: Version selection is separate policy: Cassandra last-write-wins timestamps need a total order, Dynamo and Riak can expose concurrent siblings, and a highest-version selector is Tycho guidance rather than a source guarantee.
evidence.note: Observed. Boundary: no source tests the selector; clock skew is the mechanism by which timestamps can misorder.

evidence.claim: Read repair and hinted handoff are best-effort; durability of freshness depends on anti-entropy, which is eventual.
evidence.note: Observed: Cassandra calls read repair and hinted handoff 'only best-effort' and relies on anti-entropy for eventual consistency.

evidence.claim: Atlas card states intersection alone does not guarantee freshness and lists an application-defined version selector and repair path as preconditions; sloppy quorum is the availability fallback.
evidence.note: Observed in v11 pattern atlas card: Good-fit conditions, Failure and recovery, Decision state applicable-under-conditions.

evidence.claim: Per-session read-your-writes is a weaker, separate obligation: the acknowledgement supplies a position the reader must enforce, and other sessions may still see older values.
evidence.note: Observed: write commits at 81, read at position 77 returns older title A; 'Another session can still observe 77 under this contract.' Boundary, not the quorum claim.
